Where is Salt Lake City, and how is it laid out?

Salt Lake City is Utah's capital and the county seat of Salt Lake County. It covers about 110.8 square miles in the northeast corner of the Salt Lake Valley, between the Wasatch Range on the east and the Oquirrh Mountains on the west, with the Great Salt Lake to the northwest.

Elevation averages 4,327 feet, and the Jordan River runs through the city. Wikipedia describes the eastern neighborhoods, such as the Avenues, 9th and 9th, Yalecrest, Federal Heights and Sugar House, as tending to be more affluent. The western side, including Poplar Grove, Rose Park and Glendale, tends to be more working-class and ethnically diverse.

That east and west split is useful for sellers. A house in Yalecrest and a house in Rose Park can sit in very different neighborhoods, so it helps to know which side of the city yours is on.

What is the history behind Salt Lake City's older housing?

Salt Lake City was settled in 1847 by Latter-day Saint pioneers led by Brigham Young, incorporated in 1851 and platted in 1857. It was first named Great Salt Lake City, and the word Great was dropped in 1868.

A rail line reached the city in 1870, and Utah became a state in 1896 with Salt Lake City as its capital. The Avenues is a historic district with many Victorian-era homes. Older houses can need more upkeep, and some owners decide a cash sale is easier than managing a long repair list.

What does the Wasatch Fault mean for a Salt Lake City house?

The Wasatch Fault runs along the mountain front and the Salt Lake City segment sits under the city. Wikipedia reports that this segment last produced a major earthquake about 1,200 to 1,300 years ago.

The same page cites an estimated 57 percent chance of a magnitude 6.0 or greater earthquake within 50 years, and notes that surface rupture could shift the ground by as much as 20 feet. A magnitude 5.7 quake near Magna on March 18, 2020 caused damage across the valley.

  • At least 42 percent of Wasatch Front buildings are at risk of moderate to severe damage in a strong quake.
  • Liquefaction is a risk where buildings sit on soft lake sediments.
  • Damage to gas, electric and water lines is also expected after a large quake.

None of this stops a sale, but a house with visible damage from the 2020 quake or from settling is often easier to sell as-is than to repair first.

What are Salt Lake City's climate and air quality issues?

Salt Lake City has a humid continental climate with cold winters and hot summers. The airport averages about 15.5 inches of precipitation a year and roughly 52 inches of snow, and about 127 days a year drop to freezing or below.

Mean daily highs are 38.6 degrees in January and 94.0 degrees in July. Winter temperature inversions trap pollution in the valley, and the American Lung Association ranked the city sixth-worst for air quality in 2016.

For a house, the freeze count is the practical number. Roofs, gutters, sprinkler lines and exposed pipes all see repeated freeze and thaw, so a seller who has deferred roof or plumbing work may find buyers wary.

Who employs people in Salt Lake City, and who buys homes there?

The largest employer in Salt Lake City is the Delta hub at Salt Lake City International Airport. Other major employers include Intermountain Healthcare, the University of Utah, Sinclair Oil and the LDS Church, according to Wikipedia.

The city's daytime population is above 315,000, which is well over the resident count. Westminster University and Salt Lake Community College are also based in the city. Zions Bancorporation and Questar Corporation are headquartered here, and the city was selected to host the 2034 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games.

Transit adds to the picture. TRAX light rail opened in 1999, and the S Line streetcar, formerly the Sugar House Streetcar, opened in December 2013.

Do landlords in Salt Lake City need a license?

Yes. Every residential rental property inside Salt Lake City limits needs its own current business license, according to the city's Business Licensing page.

The Landlord/Tenant Initiative, also called the Good Landlord Program, applies to single and double family homes and similar rentals. The city says taking part can reduce per-unit licensing fees by up to 95 percent, and the program's ordinance took effect on September 1, 2011.

This matters if you inherited a house that was a rental, or if you own a duplex you no longer want to manage. A cash buyer can take the property with tenants in place, and you can ask what that would mean for the lease and your license.

What are the short-term rental rules in Salt Lake City?

Short-term rentals in Salt Lake City require a business license and are allowed only in approved zoning districts. A licensee may hold only one short-term rental license in the city.

  • Each license covers one property and one dwelling unit.
  • Stays must be at least two consecutive nights.
  • Each licensed unit is limited to 200 rental nights per calendar year.
  • Owners of buildings with more than 11 units may license up to 10 percent of the units.
  • Condominium units need an HOA authorization letter.

The city's page lists the approved districts, such as MU2, MU3, D1 and GMU, so check the zoning of your address before you count on short-term rental income in a sale. For fees and dates, the city refers callers to Business Licensing at (801) 535-7980.

How does property tax work in Salt Lake City?

Salt Lake County bills Salt Lake City homes. Market value is set as of January 1, and a primary residence gets a 45 percent exemption on buildings and up to one acre of land under Utah's rules.

The Notice of Valuation and Tax Change arrives in late July. The county Board of Equalization accepts appeals from August 1 through September 15, or 45 days from the notice if that is later, and appeals need a BE01 form and evidence of value. Late appeals may be accepted until March 31 of the next year, but only on narrow grounds.

The county Treasurer says tax notices with amounts due must be mailed by November 1, and that taxes are due November 30. Unpaid taxes turn delinquent on December 1 with a penalty of the greater of 2.5 percent or $10, which drops to the greater of 1 percent or $10 if paid by January 31. The Treasurer certifies delinquent taxes on March 15, and the tax sale is traditionally held on the fourth Thursday of May.

What should a Salt Lake City seller disclose?

Utah's standard purchase contract asks sellers to disclose known problems, and the usual way to do that is a Seller's Property Condition Disclosure form. Ask your title or escrow company which disclosure forms apply to your sale.

The form covers roof leaks, flooding and drainage, mold, structural or soil problems, permits and HOA details. Because Utah has no exemption for inherited homes in that guide's description, heirs who never lived in the house should still describe what they know. When in doubt, ask a Utah real estate attorney.

The county Recorder at 2001 South State Street, Suite N1-600, keeps the property records, and its office is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Which way should a Salt Lake City seller go?

Salt Lake City sellers usually weigh a listing, a sale by owner and a cash offer. The right choice depends on condition, timing and tenants.

A listing suits a well-kept house in a strong location where you can wait for showings. A cash sale suits a house with deferred repairs, a rental with tenants, a probate property or an owner who needs a specific closing date. You can request an offer, compare it with your likely net from a listing, and say no without owing anything.

Salt Lake County. Salt Lake City is also the county seat, so the county Assessor, Treasurer and Recorder serve its homeowners.

September 15, or 45 days from the notice date if that is later. Appeals go to the Board of Equalization from August 1 and need a BE01 form with evidence supporting your value.

Do I need a license to rent out my Salt Lake City house?

Yes. Every residential rental property in the city needs a valid business license for each location. The Good Landlord Program can cut per-unit fees by up to 95 percent.

Can I run a short-term rental in Salt Lake City?

Only in approved zoning districts and with a city business license. Stays must be at least two nights, and each unit is capped at 200 rental nights a year.

Is earthquake risk a problem when selling a Salt Lake City house?

It can come up. The Wasatch Fault underlies the city, and buyers may ask about past damage. A cash buyer can purchase the house as it stands.

Where is West Valley City, Utah?

West Valley City is an inner suburb on the northwest side of the Salt Lake Valley, in Salt Lake County, and it is the second most populous city in Utah. Salt Lake City borders it to the north, South Salt Lake to the east, Magna to the west, and Taylorsville and Kearns to the south.

The Oquirrh Mountains are to the west and the Jordan River forms the eastern edge. Elevation is about 4,304 feet and the city covers roughly 35.5 to 35.9 square miles, depending on which source you read.

The 2020 census counted 140,230 residents, up 8.3% from 129,480 in 2010. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate shown on this page is 137,491, which is slightly below the 2020 count.

How was West Valley City formed?

West Valley City incorporated in 1980 by merging four unincorporated communities: Hunter, Granger, Chesterfield and Redwood. The land west of the Jordan River was first staked out by Joseph Harker and his family, and Granger was settled in 1849 by Welsh pioneers who came with Dan Jones.

Hunter was settled in 1876 and began irrigating in 1881, with fruit trees as the main crop. Growth took off in the 1970s, and the city had 72,299 people at its first census in 1980.

West Valley City hosted men's and women's ice hockey for the 2002 Olympic Winter Games. In 2011 it began planning a downtown district around Fairbourne Station, with a civic center, hotels, a plaza and a transit hub.

West Valley City itself employed 909, and Sutter Health and USANA Health Sciences were also on the list. Companies based in the city include Backcountry.com, Black Rifle Coffee Company, C.R. England, FranklinCovey and USANA. These figures are from 2017, so treat them as a snapshot rather than a current count.

The Maverik Center is home to the Salt Lake City Stars of the NBA G League, and the USANA Amphitheatre and the Utah Cultural Celebration Center add event traffic near Valley Fair Mall.

What roads and transit serve West Valley City?

Interstate 215, State Route 172 (5600 West) and State Route 171 (3500 South) are the main roads, and the Utah Transit Authority runs an intermodal hub in the city. West Valley Central station is on the TRAX Green Line.

The 3500 South MAX bus rapid transit line serves the area, and the Midvalley Express connects West Valley Central and 2700 West to Taylorsville and on to Murray Central station. A planned Hunter Town Center near 5600 West and 3500 South had not been built as of the source.

Which school district covers West Valley City?

West Valley City is in the Granite School District, which serves about 67,000 students across central Salt Lake County. The district lists nine high schools, and Granger High School and Hunter High School are both in West Valley City.

Granger Senior High opened in 1958 and Hunter High in 1990. Charter schools in the city include East Hollywood High School (film education), American Preparatory Academy and Monticello Academy.

As in any city, the school boundary depends on the address. The district can confirm it before you advertise the house.

What rental and code rules apply in West Valley City?

Every owner of a rental dwelling in West Valley City must hold a current West Valley City business license. An owner with several units needs only one license if they give the city a complete, current list of the units and pay the fees. When a property has more than one owner, each is jointly and severally liable for the fees and any penalties.

The city's code also sets a rental nuisance standard. More than two police calls for one rental unit in 12 months counts as excessive calls, and an unresolved notice of violation is one with no recorded notice of compliance. The city's ordinance enforcement division handles abatement of unsightly or hazardous property and rental licensing.

  • Clear any open notice of violation and record the notice of compliance.
  • Gather the unit list if you own more than one rental in the city.

Salt Lake County property tax is due November 30, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on December 1. Notices are mailed by November 1, and the 45-day appeal window runs from August 1 to September 15. Properties more than five years delinquent go to a tax sale in late May.

A primary residence in Utah is taxed on 55% of its market value because of the 45% exemption. A second residence or an unoccupied house is taxed at the full value.

Deeds are recorded at the Salt Lake County Recorder, 2001 South State Street, Suite N1-600. The flat fee is $40.00, the deed should list the parcel number and the grantee's mailing address, and it needs a notary acknowledgment. The same office keeps the ownership records the city code uses to identify an owner.

The weather is the same as elsewhere in the valley, with average highs of 94.0 degrees in July and 38.6 in January at Salt Lake City, about 15.5 inches of precipitation and strong winter inversions which puts steady wear on roofs and heating and cooling systems.

Where is West Jordan, Utah, and what borders it?

West Jordan sits at the southwest end of the Salt Lake Valley in Salt Lake County, with the Jordan River as its eastern edge and the Oquirrh Mountains on the west. Taylorsville and Kearns lie to the north, South Jordan to the south, and Sandy, Murray and Midvale to the east.

The city covers roughly 31 to 32 square miles, depending on which figure you use, and the elevation is a little over 4,300 feet. Western neighborhoods such as Welby, Copper Hills and Jordan Hills climb the lower slopes of the Oquirrh range, so views and drainage differ a lot from the flat blocks near the river.

The 2020 census counted 116,961 people, which made West Jordan the third largest city in Utah. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate on this page is 116,812, so growth has leveled off after the jump from 68,336 in 2000 to 103,712 in 2010.

How did West Jordan start, and what changed in 2020?

Settlers arrived in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, and the river west of Salt Lake City came to be called the Jordan. Archibald Gardner built one of the area's first sawmills in 1850, and his mill and houses were later turned into Gardner Village, a shopping district.

West Jordan was incorporated on January 10, 1941. Its population was only 2,107 in 1950 and 4,221 in 1970, then 27,192 in 1980 and 42,892 in 1990. Much of the city's housing was therefore built after 1980.

In November 2017 voters approved a council-mayor form of government, effective January 6, 2020. The mayor, Dirk Burton, serves a term running 2020 to 2028, and a seven-member council has four district seats and three at-large seats.

The Mountain View Corridor, a ten-lane route with exits at 7800 South, 9000 South and Old Bingham Highway, opened its first phase on December 15, 2012. A TRAX light rail line opened August 7, 2011, and has six stops in West Jordan on its way from Fashion Place West in Murray to Daybreak in South Jordan.

Distance to a station or an on-ramp is one of the first things buyers check. Houses beside Bangerter Highway or Redwood Road may carry traffic noise, while houses a short walk from a rail stop draw a different crowd.

Most of West Jordan is in the Jordan School District, and two small northern sections are in the Granite School District. Jordan School District has its headquarters at 7387 S Campus View Drive in West Jordan and enrolled about 57,866 students in 2021 and 2022.

The city has 16 elementary schools, four middle schools and two high schools, West Jordan High School and Copper Hills High School. The Jordan District lost 44 of its 84 schools in 2009 when the eastern communities formed the Canyons School District.

Ask the district to confirm the school boundary for a specific address, because a house on a district edge may feed a different school than the neighbor across the street.

Renewal of the class is required every four years.

The city states that single-family rentals average 78% more police and fire calls a year than owner-occupied homes, and it wants at least one off-street parking space per rental unit at no extra charge. Code enforcement is at 8000 S. Redwood Road, and the main phone line is 801-569-5000. Residents can file complaints through the city's online Report a Problem form.

If you rent your West Jordan house, confirm that your license is current before you sell.

Provo is the southern end of the FrontRunner commuter rail line, which has served the city since December 10, 2012. The Provo Intermodal Center ties together rail, local UTA buses and Greyhound, and Amtrak's California Zephyr stops at the Provo station daily.

The statute, as that article describes it, reaches parcels of 11,000 square feet or larger with a single-family home, and cities had to amend their policies by October 1. Utah County assesses and bills Provo property taxes, and the county Auditor sits at 100 East Center Street, Suite 3600, in Provo itself. Valuation notices go out at the end of July, and a market-value appeal to the Board of Equalization must be filed by September 15, online, by email, by mail or in person.

The tax notice follows in mid to late October. A primary residence is taxed on 55% of its market value because of the 45% exemption, as long as someone lives there at least 183 consecutive days a year. A rental occupied full-time by a tenant can qualify, while a vacant or part-time rental is treated as secondary and taxed on full value. Provo's large rental share makes that rule matter. The Treasurer can be reached at 801-851-8255 for payoff amounts on delinquent tax.

What do Provo sellers usually face, and how does a cash sale work?

Common Provo situations include a house with tenants, a rental that has outlived its license, an inherited property, and a house that needs repairs. A cash sale to us follows a short path: you tell us about the house, we review it, and we make an offer based on condition.

Why is Provo's owner-occupancy rate so low?

Where is St. George, Utah, and how big is it?

St. George sits in the southwest corner of Utah, on the Arizona border, and is the county seat of Washington County. It is on Interstate 15, about 118 miles northeast of Las Vegas and 300 miles south-southwest of Salt Lake City, at an elevation of 2,530 feet.

The city covers roughly 77 square miles in the northeastern edge of the Mojave Desert, just south of the Pine Valley Mountains. The Virgin River and Santa Clara River both run through the valley, and Fort Pearce Wash carries water during storms. Zion National Park lies to the east and Snow Canyon State Park is close to town.

The Census Bureau counted 95,342 residents in 2020 and estimates 108,713 for July 1, 2025. That is a jump of about 13,000 people in five years, which tells you how many houses have gone up in recent years.

What is the history of St. George?

St. George began in 1861 as a cotton mission. About 300 families were called to settle the area at the church conference of October 6, 1861, under apostle Erastus Snow. The city was named for apostle George A. Smith and was incorporated on January 17, 1862.

Cotton never paid off, but the nickname "Utah's Dixie" stuck. The St. George Utah Temple was finished in April 1877 and is the oldest temple in the church still in use. Much of the housing around it is far newer, since the population has roughly doubled since 2000 (49,728 residents then, 95,342 in 2020).

The valley has had its share of natural events. A 1992 earthquake caused about $1 million in damage and destroyed three houses. In January 2005 a regional flood killed one person and destroyed 28 homes along the Santa Clara River. Both are reminders to check a property's flood and soil history before you set a price.

The St. George economy leans on tourism, manufacturing and new-home construction. More than a dozen golf courses stay open year-round, and the city is a well-known retirement destination.

Big events bring crowds, including the St. George Marathon, the Ironman triathlon and the Huntsman World Senior Games. A house near a venue or a course can draw visitors, but it can also bring traffic and noise that buyers weigh.

An added fee for heavy water use began in 2023, and the money pays for rebates to replace grass with water-efficient landscaping. The district projected savings of nearly 11 billion gallons over ten years.

The reports we reviewed did not spell out how the rules apply to older houses. If your yard has a large lawn, ask the city or your water provider what applies before you spend money on landscaping to sell.

Public high schools in the Washington County School District include Desert Hills, Dixie, Pine View, Snow Canyon and Crimson Cliffs. Which one serves the house is often a first question from a family moving in.

Washington County property taxes are due November 30 each year, even when you do not get a notice. The county treasurer says taxes are a lien on the property, not on a person, so an unpaid bill stays with the house when it sells.

The title company prorates the bill at closing, and your settlement statement shows each side's share. Under Utah Code section 59-2-1331, a payment after the due date is delinquent and carries a 2.5% penalty or $10, whichever is greater, which falls to 1% if everything is paid by January 31.

  • Treasurer: 111 East Tabernacle St., St. George, (435) 301-7720. Partial payments of $10 or more per parcel are accepted at any time.

Utah gives a 45% exemption on a primary residence, up to one acre. Rental homes can qualify, while vacation homes and time-shares do not, so a second home in St. George is taxed on its full value. Ask the Washington County assessor how your parcel is classified.

What do St. George sellers usually face?

St. George has an older population than most Utah cities, with 21.8% of residents age 65 or older and a reputation as a retirement destination. That means downsizing moves and inherited houses are part of the picture here.

Pioneers settled the Lehi area in fall 1850 at a place called Dry Creek, and the Utah Territorial Legislature incorporated Lehi City on February 5, 1852, making it the sixth city incorporated in Utah. A change of ownership can trigger a declaration form for the new owner. The big residential wave came much later. Wikipedia lists the population at 6,438 in 1970 and 52,210 in 1980, a gain of more than 45,000 residents in ten years. The city reached 96,904 residents in the 2020 census, up 10.8 percent from 87,461 in 2010.

Where is Layton, Utah, and how is the city laid out?

Layton is a city in Davis County on the northern Wasatch Front, about 25 miles north of Salt Lake City and 15 miles south of Ogden. Its elevation is roughly 4,459 feet, and the city covers a little over 22 square miles.

Hill Air Force Base sits on the northern edge. Clearfield lies to the northwest, South Weber to the northeast, Kaysville to the south and Syracuse to the west. The Wasatch Mountains rise along the eastern side, and the Great Salt Lake wetlands lie to the southwest.

On the map, the east side climbs toward the foothills and Adams Canyon. The middle follows the I-15 corridor, where shopping and hotels cluster. The west side runs flatter toward Syracuse and the lake wetlands.

Winters bring lake effect snow, summers run hot, and a roof or furnace that is near the end of its life tends to show up in a buyer's inspection. Sellers with an older house often decide whether to repair or sell as-is at that point.

How did Layton grow from a farm settlement into Davis County's largest city?

Layton was settled in the 1850s as an outgrowth of Kaysville and takes its name from Christopher Layton, a Latter-day Saint settler and leader. The two communities clashed in the 1880s over taxes, and the dispute reached the U.S. Supreme Court in 1894 in Linford v. Ellison, which sided with the Layton property owners.

Layton became its own unincorporated area in 1902 and an incorporated town in 1920. The population stayed near 600 until 1940, when Hill Field opened to the north and workers began moving in. Layton was counted at 3,456 people in 1950 and has been growing since.

  • 1960: 9,027 residents
  • 1990: 41,784 residents
  • 2000: 58,474 residents
  • 2020: 81,773 residents

Layton passed Bountiful in 1985 to become the most populous city in Davis County, and it now ranks ninth in the state. The Census Bureau puts the July 2025 estimate at 85,308.

Because so much of the housing stock went up in waves tied to base employment and commuter growth, a single street can mix 1960s ramblers with homes from the 1990s and later subdivisions. Condition varies a lot from block to block.

What drives Layton's economy, and why does Hill Air Force Base matter to sellers?

Hill Air Force Base is the anchor employer next door to Layton, and Wikipedia describes it as the sixth largest employer in Utah as of 2018. The base opened as Hill Field on November 7, 1940, and became Hill Air Force Base on February 5, 1948.

The Ogden Air Logistics Complex there provides engineering and logistics management for aircraft such as the F-35, F-16 and A-10. Base host units include the 75th Air Base Wing and the 388th and 419th Fighter Wings. Assignments, deployments and retirements create regular turnover in local housing.

Beyond the base, the city's own economic pages and reference sources point to a retail and hospitality district around I-15. It includes Layton Hills Mall, a stretch of chain restaurants known as Restaurant Row, more than 1,000 hotel beds and the Davis Conference Center. East Gate Business Park and a Weber State University campus add other jobs and a student population.

An owner who has to move by a fixed date, such as a transfer, can find it hard to line that up with a listing that may sit for weeks. A cash buyer can often work to a closing date the seller picks.

Which roads, rail and schools shape Layton neighborhoods?

I-15 runs through the center of Layton with interchanges at Antelope Drive, Hillfield Road and Layton Parkway. US-89 follows the eastern edge near the foothills, SR-193 runs east and west past the base's south gate, and SR-177 serves the western side.

FrontRunner commuter rail stops at Layton Station, built where the old Union Pacific depot stood, and Utah Transit Authority runs buses. Homes within easy reach of the station or an I-15 ramp appeal to commuters headed for Salt Lake City or Ogden.

Layton is served by Davis School District. Layton High School opened in 1966 and Northridge High School in 1992, and the Northern Utah Academy for Math, Engineering and Science is an early college charter school partnered with Weber State. Buyers often ask which school boundary a house sits in, so confirm the address with the district rather than relying on a listing description.

City amenities that pull in buyers include Layton Commons Park, Ellison Park, Legacy Park and Veterans Park, the Edward A. Kenley Centennial Amphitheater and the Layton Utah Temple, dedicated on June 16, 2024.

What does Layton code enforcement check before you sell?

Layton code enforcement is run through the police department and focuses on exterior conditions such as weeds, junk and vehicles. A violation can slow a sale if a buyer or lender notices it, and unpaid abatement costs can follow the owner.

  • Weeds and grass must stay at 12 inches or shorter.
  • Junk, appliances, tires and building materials cannot be stored outdoors unless they are fully inside a structure with walls and a roof.
  • Vehicles must be licensed and operable, and must park on a hard surface. A vehicle with registration expired four months or more must be removed or enclosed.
  • Trees and bushes must be trimmed to at least 7 feet above sidewalks and 13 feet 6 inches above streets.

The usual process starts with a 14-day courtesy notice. After a re-inspection, a Notice of Ordinance Violation can go to the City Attorney's Office. If an owner never cleans up, a judge can order the city to remove the violations and bill the owner plus an administrative fee.

An owner of a vacant or inherited house who lives elsewhere may miss these notices. Reach the department at codeenforcement@laytoncityutah.gov or (801) 497-8300 to check whether anything is open on a property.

How do Davis County valuation notices and tax dates affect a Layton sale?

Davis County mails its Notice of Assessors' Property Market Valuation at the end of July, and the appeal window closes in mid-September. The county's appeals page gives September 15, 2026 as the late-appeal date but also says September 16 in its instructions, so check the exact day with the office.

The Davis County Commission sits as the Board of Equalization. An appeal can challenge only market value, not the tax rate, and the owner or an authorized agent with a notarized authorization must file. Accepted evidence includes closing documents, a certified appraisal, three or more comparable sales near January 1, or documented errors in the assessor's data.

Tax Administration is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101, Farmington, and can be reached at 801-451-3331 or taxadmin@daviscountyutah.gov. A recent sale price on a closing statement is the kind of record that supports a value discussion.

What happens to the primary residence exemption when a Layton house sells?

Utah gives a 45 percent exemption on the market value of a primary residence, so the taxable value is 55 percent of market value. The home must be occupied at least 183 consecutive days in a calendar year, and a household can claim only one such exemption.

The Utah State Tax Commission says the exemption does not carry over automatically after a sale or deed transfer. New owners file Form TC-473A with the county Board of Equalization by September 15, and counties cannot accept late applications. Under amended Utah Code 59-2-103.5, owners must file that form in these situations starting January 1, 2027.

For a seller this mostly matters in how a buyer reads the numbers. A house that was taxed at 55 percent of value can be taxed at 100 percent for a year if the new owner files late.

How does a cash sale of a Layton house work?

A cash sale in Layton follows the same title steps as any other sale, but the buyer does not need a mortgage approval. The seller signs a purchase contract, a title company searches for liens, and the deed is recorded with the Davis County Recorder in Farmington.

  • Share the address, the condition and any deadline, such as a base transfer or a code notice.
  • Review the offer and the closing date the buyer proposes.
  • Sign the contract and let the title company clear liens, unpaid property taxes and any open code charges.
  • Sign the deed at closing and receive the proceeds after payoffs.

Davis County lists a Property Watch email alert on its site that tells an owner when a title on a parcel changes. Sellers who are away from Layton, or who inherited a house, can sign up so they hear about any change.

More questions about Layton, UT

How big is Layton, Utah?

Layton is the largest city in Davis County. The 2020 census counted 81,773 residents, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 85,308.

Does Hill Air Force Base affect Layton home sales?

Yes, indirectly. Hill AFB borders Layton and is one of the largest employers in Utah, so base moves and retirements regularly bring owners who need to sell or buy on a set schedule.

When are Davis County property tax valuation notices mailed?

They are mailed at the end of July each year. The appeal deadline falls in mid-September, and the county page lists September 15, 2026 for late appeals, so confirm the exact date with the Tax Administration office at 801-451-3331.

Can code enforcement notices be fixed before selling a house in Layton?

Yes. Layton starts with a 14-day courtesy notice, and many items such as weeds, junk or an inoperable vehicle can be cleared in that window. Email codeenforcement@laytoncityutah.gov to ask what is open on an address.

Does a buyer keep the primary residence exemption on a Layton house?

No, not automatically. The Utah State Tax Commission says new owners must file Form TC-473A by September 15 to receive the 45 percent exemption, and a late filing can mean being taxed at full market value for that year.

  • Transient room tax records, if you ever rented the house for stays under 30 days.
  • Any HOA contact, loan payoff details and the roof's age.

Eagle Mountain also has four regional parks and about 35 local parks, and the Mountain Ranch Bike Park opened in 2009 as the first of its kind on the Wasatch Front. Neighborhood amenities like these are worth a line in any listing or offer discussion.

November 30. Utah County lists that date as the due date for real property taxes, and delinquent parcels are penalized beginning December 1.

The Lake Mountain School District. It takes over from Alpine School District on July 1, 2027 and also covers Saratoga Springs, Cedar Fort and Fairfield.

For a seller, newer construction usually means fewer old-house surprises. A house that needs work, or has a tenant or a title problem, is the kind of listing a financed buyer tends to pass over.

The settlement dates to 1851, when Henry Harriman, Thomas Jefferson Butterfield, John Jay Stocking and Robert Cowan Petty established it. Fort Herriman stood where the community garden is today, and only two black locust trees remain from that era.

Residents petitioned for incorporation in 1999, and Herriman became a city on April 19, 2001.

Yes, to a degree. Herriman is described as highly susceptible to fire because of exposed mountains, dry brush and open fields. In 2010 a fire that started during a National Guard exercise at nearby Camp Williams burned about 3,500 acres.

Utah's House Bill 48 of 2025 also led to a statewide map that scores buildings from 1 (lowest) to 8 (highest) for wildfire exposure. You can search an address at wildfirerisk.utah.gov to see its score.

The city also warns that work done without a permit may require removing finishes such as drywall and insulation for inspection. If your basement apartment was finished without paperwork, that is the cost to weigh before you list.

How do Herriman property taxes and recording work?

November 30. Salt Lake County lists that as the last day to pay without penalty, and unpaid taxes are delinquent from December 1.

Taxes become delinquent if not paid by November 30. The penalty is 2.5 percent or $10, whichever is greater, per parcel, falling to 1 percent or $10 if paid by January 31. The Utah County Board of Equalization is at 111 South University Avenue in Provo.

Where is Logan, Utah, and what is the land like?

Logan is the county seat of Cache County, about 47 miles north of Ogden and 82 miles north of Salt Lake City. It sits on the Logan River near the eastern edge of Cache Valley, on the western slopes of the Bear River Mountains.

The elevation is about 4,534 feet, and Mount Logan rises to 9,710 feet to the east. Streets on the east side climb across terraces called benches, which are old Lake Bonneville sediment that the river cut through after the lake drained roughly 14,500 years ago. West of town the ground flattens into farmland and marsh, and newer subdivisions have been spreading north and south.

Where a house sits on that terrain shapes what an inspector looks at. Lots on the benches face slope and runoff questions, and lots in the flat west sit closer to farmland and marsh.

What are winters like in Logan, and what do they do to a house?

Logan has a humid continental climate with warm, usually dry summers and cold winters that bring moderate snow. Annual precipitation averages about 18.97 inches and snowfall about 61.5 inches. The record low is minus 25 degrees and the record high is 103.

Roofs carry snow load for months, and pipes in vacant houses can freeze. Winter temperature inversions can trap cold air and pollutants in the valley. An owner who cannot heat or check on a vacant house through the cold months may prefer to close before winter.

Brigham Young sent settlers in 1859 to survey a fort site near the Logan River, and the town was named for Ephraim Logan, an early fur trapper. Logan was incorporated on January 17, 1866, and Alvin Crockett was elected its first mayor on March 5, 1866.

  • 1883: the Cache County Historic Courthouse was built.

That college is now Utah State University. Cache County itself covers 1,173 square miles and borders Idaho, and Logan became its county seat in 1857. The county leads Utah in dairy products and is a major producer of hay, alfalfa and grain.

The 2020 census counted 52,778 people in Logan, up from 48,174 in 2010. The Census Bureau estimates 55,576 as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 median age was 24.2 and the city is home to Utah State University.

Where is Draper, Utah, and why does the county line matter when you sell?

Draper sits on the Wasatch Front about 20 miles south of Salt Lake City, and the city spans two counties: Salt Lake County and Utah County. It covers roughly 30 square miles at an elevation of 4,751 feet, with Sandy to the north, South Jordan to the northwest, Riverton and Bluffdale to the west, and Lehi, Highland and Alpine to the south and southeast.

The city describes itself as sitting at the Point of the Mountain, the narrow gap between the south end of the Salt Lake Valley and the north end of Utah Valley. For a seller, the county line decides which assessor values the house, which treasurer sends the tax bill and which recorder files the deed. The school district changes too: the Salt Lake County side is served by Canyons School District and the Utah County side by Alpine School District.

Check your parcel number before you plan anything. Two neighbors a few blocks apart can deal with different county offices, different tax calendars and different school boundaries.

What is the history of Draper in brief?

Draper began as a cattle and farming settlement in the fall of 1849, when Ebenezer Brown grazed cattle near South Willow Creek. His wife's brother, William Draper Jr., joined the family in 1850, and about twenty families lived in the area by the end of 1852.

The first post office opened in 1854 under the name Draperville. That same year Ebenezer Brown gave land near 12650 South 900 East for a fort, though the walls were never finished. By the 1940s the town was known as the Egg Basket of Utah, and Draper became a city in 1978.

The growth since then is striking. The 2020 census counted 51,017 people in Draper, up from 7,257 in 1990. Many of the neighborhoods you see today were built in that window, so houses in the city range from old farm lots to subdivisions less than a generation old.

What does the Draper economy look like?

Draper is part of the Silicon Slopes tech corridor, and the city reports more than 1,000 businesses. Company headquarters or major offices named in public sources include 1-800 Contacts, Control4, HealthEquity, Pluralsight and Synchrony Bank, along with Dealertrack, Trader Joe's and Tesla in the city's own list. Utah's first IKEA opened in Draper in 2007.

The Utah State Prison operated in Draper from 1951 to 2022, and it ranked in the top employer size band (1,000 to 1,999 workers) in a fiscal 2018 snapshot.

Getting around is straightforward by Utah standards. Interstate 15 runs through the area, UTA's TRAX Blue Line stops at Draper Town Center and Kimballs Lane, and a FrontRunner commuter rail station is also in the city. Salt Lake International Airport and Provo Municipal Airport are each about 30 minutes away by car, according to the city.

Does wildfire risk affect a Draper house sale?

It can, especially for homes along the foothills. In December 2025 the Draper City Council adopted Ordinance 1695, which created a Wildland Urban Interface Area in the city code. The public notice does not map the boundaries or list the rules, so ask the city for the full ordinance if your lot backs onto open hillside.

A separate state program adds another layer. Utah House Bill 48 of 2025 led the state forestry division to publish a wildfire risk map that scores each building from 1 to 8. A building that scores 7 or higher and sits within 250 meters of at least two other buildings falls inside the high-risk boundary, and owners of those buildings may owe the state an annual fee once the program starts, which the state expected later in 2026.

  • Look up the address at wildfirerisk.utah.gov before you list or accept an offer.

What are Draper's rules for short-term rentals and accessory units?

Draper requires two approvals to run a short-term rental: a business license and a short-term rental permit. A stay counts as short term when it is under 30 consecutive days, the minimum stay is two nights, and the permit has to be renewed every year. Each day of unpermitted operation is a separate violation.

Accessory dwelling units have their own limits.

  • A detached ADU needs a residential lot of at least 12,000 square feet.
  • An internal ADU generally needs a residential lot over 6,000 square feet on a qualifying street, and the city has mapped areas where internal units are banned.
  • The owner must live in the main dwelling for both types.
  • Rentals of an ADU must run at least 30 consecutive days, and each needs one extra on-site parking space.

A basement apartment that was built without a permit is a common snag. The city's ADU page says owners who did not apply by February 1, 2022 face immediate enforcement, so a buyer who needs financing may hesitate over one. Draper's planning office takes questions at (801) 576-6399.

How are property taxes handled on a Draper home?

Your county's calendar controls the bill, and Utah gives primary residences a 45% exemption so that only 55% of market value is taxed. Rental homes can qualify as primary residences under the state's rules, while vacation homes cannot.

For a Salt Lake County parcel, the county lists these dates:

  • July 22: valuation notices are mailed.
  • August 1 to September 15: the Board of Equalization takes valuation appeals.
  • November 1: official tax notices go out.
  • November 30: last day to pay without penalty.
  • December 1: unpaid taxes become delinquent, with a penalty of the greater of 2.5% or $10 per parcel.

A Utah County parcel follows the same November 30 due date, with notices mailed around the third week of October. Delinquent parcels in Utah County face a penalty of $10 or 1%, whichever is greater, on December 1. If your house is on the market when the notice arrives, tell the title officer so the current-year bill is handled correctly at closing.

How does a cash sale work in Draper?

A cash sale in Draper follows the same steps as any Utah sale, minus the lender. You give us the address and a few details, we review the house, and if the offer works you pick the closing date with a title company.

  2. We look at the property and the recent sales around it.
  3. You decide whether to accept the offer or walk away.
  4. A title company runs the title search and prepares the closing paperwork.
  5. The deed is recorded with the county recorder where the parcel sits.

Recording is cheap. Salt Lake County charges a flat $40 recording fee, and Utah County lists the same $40 standard fee per document. Salt Lake County asks for a notary acknowledgment, the grantee's address and the tax serial number on the deed.

What do Draper sellers usually run into?

A short list of issues tends to slow a Draper sale.

  • A hillside lot with a high state wildfire score.
  • An older basement unit with no ADU permit.
  • A short-term rental permit that lapsed after its annual renewal.
  • A tenant in place on a rental, since roughly 31% of occupied homes are not owner-occupied.
  • Confusion over whether the parcel is billed by Salt Lake County or Utah County.

Any of these can be solved, but each adds steps to a traditional listing. A direct sale lets you sell the house as it stands and deal with the paperwork at the title company.

Is Draper in Salt Lake County or Utah County?

Both. Draper lies in Salt Lake County and Utah County, so the county for your tax bill and deed depends on the parcel. Look up the parcel number on your tax notice to see which county applies.

When are Draper property taxes due?

November 30, whichever county bills you. Salt Lake County lists November 30 as the last day to pay without penalty, and Utah County does the same. If the date falls on a weekend or holiday it moves to the next business day.

Do I need a permit to rent my Draper house on a short-term basis?

Yes. Draper requires both a business license and a short-term rental permit, and the permit must be renewed each year. Operating without both is a violation, and each day counts separately.

Can I sell a Draper house that has an unpermitted basement apartment?

Yes, you can sell it, but expect questions. Draper requires an ADU permit before an accessory unit is rented, and the owner must live in the main dwelling. A cash buyer can take the house as it is, while a bank-financed buyer may ask you to resolve the permit first.

How do I check wildfire risk for a Draper address?

Search the address at wildfirerisk.utah.gov. The portal shows a structure exposure score from 1 to 8, and the state treats buildings scoring 7 or higher near other buildings as high risk.

Where is Riverton, Utah?

Riverton is a city in Salt Lake County, in the southwestern corner of the Salt Lake Valley about 20 miles south and slightly west of Salt Lake City. It covers 12.58 square miles at 4,439 feet, and it borders South Jordan to the north, Draper to the east, Bluffdale to the south and Herriman to the west.

This is a different part of Utah from Orem, Provo and Pleasant Grove. Riverton is in Salt Lake County rather than Utah County, so its property tax, appeals and deed recording run through county offices in Salt Lake City, not Provo.

How did Riverton grow from a farm town to a suburb?

Riverton began as a farming community settled in the mid-1850s, probably first by Archibald Gardner, and it was originally called Gardnerville. Residents farmed alfalfa, wheat, sugar beets, tomatoes, poultry, sheep and dairy, and Jordan Valley Bank started as a community bank here in 1905.

Electricity arrived in 1912, and the Salt Lake and Utah Railroad (Orem Line) ran through town from 1914 to 1945. The city incorporated in the late 1940s. A 1996 annexation nearly doubled its size, and Herriman's incorporation in 2000 fixed the western boundary. Farm numbers in the county fell from 2,595 in 1950 to 798 in 1969. The old Riverton Elementary School became the Riverton Community Center and City Hall by 2005 to 2006.

The city grew in pieces over time, so the year a house was built depends heavily on which part of Riverton it sits in.

Riverton's main roads are Bangerter Highway, the Mountain View Corridor and Redwood Road, and drivers reach Interstate 15 through 12300 South or Bangerter Highway. Bangerter Highway (SR-154) enters Riverton as it curves north and crosses 13400 South, 12600 South and 11400 South, and the 12600 South interchange opened on May 19, 2022.

Transit is limited. UTA Route 126 started in April 2025 and runs hourly along 12600 South. Riverton workers average 24.8 minutes to work.

The 2019 draft proposed a 650 square foot limit, one parking space, an owner living on the property and one family in the unit. Residents argued the draft was too tight, and the council debated capping size at half the home instead. Salt Lake County assesses Riverton property, with a Notice of Valuation and Tax Change mailed in late July. The Board of Equalization accepts appeals from August 1 through September 15, and the deadline is 45 days from the notice or September 15, whichever is longer.

  • File online, by mail with form BE01, or in person at 2001 South State Street, Suite N3-300, Salt Lake City.

Where is American Fork, Utah?

American Fork is a city in north-central Utah County, at the foot of Mount Timpanogos in the Wasatch Range and just north of Utah Lake. It sits about 32 miles southeast of Salt Lake City, at an elevation near 4,600 feet, and its ZIP code is 84003.

The city belongs to the Provo-Orem metropolitan area. Lehi, Pleasant Grove, Highland, Alpine and Cedar Hills are nearby cities in the same part of the county. Utah County itself covers about 2,144 square miles and is anchored by Provo, home to Brigham Young University.

The Census Bureau counted 33,337 residents in 2020 and estimates 41,020 as of July 1, 2025, so the city has grown by nearly a quarter in five years.

How did American Fork start, and where does the name come from?

Mormon pioneers settled American Fork in the summer of 1850 and named it for American Fork Creek, one of the streams that feed Utah Lake. Stephen Chipman, Arza Adams and the Eldredge families were among the first.

Residents planned a town called Lake City in 1852, and the Utah legislature incorporated it on June 4, 1853. The name reverted to American Fork in 1860 to stop mail from being confused with Salt Lake City. In July 1853, residents voted to build a fort enclosing about 37 acres, and most families lived inside for roughly three years.

The mid-twentieth century changed the town. Columbia Steel built a plant in 1942 and 1943, which later became Geneva Steel, and the housing boom that followed pushed the population to about 4,500. The plant closed in November 2001, and the city still holds an annual Steel Days celebration. A city-owned hospital opened on Main Street in 1937, and Intermountain Health Care bought it in 1977.

The commute is short by metro standards, and rail is part of it. FrontRunner commuter rail opened an American Fork station in 2012, and the line runs from Provo to Ogden through Orem, Vineyard, American Fork and Lehi. Interstate 15 was widened through Utah County in a project completed in 2012.

The Census puts the mean commute for workers at 23.3 minutes, and Salt Lake City is about 32 miles away. A house near the FrontRunner station or the freeway has an access story worth mentioning to buyers.

What is American Fork Canyon, and does it matter to sellers?

American Fork Canyon is the Wasatch canyon above the city, and it holds Timpanogos Cave National Monument, which was designated on October 14, 1922. The monument's 1.5-mile trail to the cave entrance gains 1,092 feet, and the National Park Service counted 92,031 visitors in 2025.

The creek that runs down the canyon becomes the American Fork River at its mouth. A mountain backdrop is a selling point for houses on the east side of town, and the canyon draws hikers every summer. Buyers who value trail access will ask how far the house is from the canyon road.

American Fork's public schools now belong to the Alpine School District, and that district is dissolving on July 1, 2027. A Daily Herald report from June 2026 says American Fork will be in a new district called Aspen Peaks, along with Lehi, Highland, Alpine and Cedar Hills. The other two new districts are Lake Mountain and Timpanogos.

American Fork High School and American Fork Junior High are the city's main secondary schools, and the elementary schools include Barratt, Forbes, Greenwood, Legacy and Shelley. Utah County approved the new boundaries in March 2025, and they largely follow city lines. Buyers with children will ask about this change, so tell them which district the house falls in and check the county's boundary maps for border lots.

What should you know about American Fork utilities?

Two utility details are worth knowing before you list: the city's pressurized irrigation system and the sewer treatment charges.

  • The city's pressurized irrigation system delivers untreated water for lawns and gardens. Construction ran from 2007 to 2010, and the city's water conservation plan says about 95% of residents are connected. Meters are installed on connections, and billing by usage was planned to begin with the 2025 irrigation season.
  • Sewer treatment comes from the Timpanogos Special Service District, which serves American Fork and several neighbors. It raised rates 40% on January 1, 2024, 15% in 2025 and another 15% on January 1, 2026. American Fork says the city's own sewer charges did not change.
  • The 2024 conservation plan lists a single-family base water rate of $16.17 a month for a three-quarter-inch meter, with no volume charge for the first 3,000 gallons.

City Hall is at 51 East Main Street, and the phone is 801-763-3000. The city's online Report a Concern form takes code enforcement, road, sidewalk and sewer complaints.

How does property tax work in American Fork?

American Fork is in Utah County, so the Utah County Assessor, Auditor and Treasurer handle your bill. The Assessor sets market value, the Auditor mails the Notice of Property Valuation and Tax Changes each July, and the Treasurer sends the tax notice in mid to late October.

Owner-occupied and long-term rental homes can receive the primary residential exemption, which taxes 55% of market value. A primary residence is one occupied for at least 183 consecutive days in a year. After a purchase or ownership change, the county sends a Residential Property Declaration to the owner. Sellers should tell buyers to watch for that letter and return it on time.

American Fork lies on the Wasatch Front, where the Provo segment of the Wasatch Fault produced a major earthquake about 200 to 700 years ago. The fault as a whole is about 240 miles long, and about 80% of Utah's people live along it.

The Utah County Recorder records the deed at the Provo address above. The office does not prepare or notarize documents, give legal advice, or search title, so the title company or an attorney handles that step.

A cash sale is a normal closing without a lender. The buyer and seller sign a purchase agreement, a title company opens escrow and runs the title search, payoff demands go out for any mortgage or lien, and the deed is recorded in Provo.

Yes, for primary residences and long-term rentals. The exemption lowers taxable value to 55% of market value, and the home must be occupied at least 183 consecutive days in a year. After a sale, the new owner may need to file a declaration.

Where is Syracuse, Utah, and what sits around it?

Syracuse is in northern Davis County, on the east shore of the Great Salt Lake, about 30 miles north of Salt Lake City. The city lies between the lake and Interstate 15, at an elevation of 4,272 feet, and covers about 10 square miles.

Neighbors are West Point to the north, Clearfield to the east and northeast, and Layton to the southeast. Syracuse calls itself the Gateway to Antelope Island, and a causeway off State Route 127 connects the city to Antelope Island State Park in the lake. For a seller, the setting matters in two ways. Buyers like the lake and island access, and the land on the west side of town has wetlands that affect what can be built.

How did Syracuse grow from a farm town into a city?

Syracuse was settled in 1878 and took its name from Syracuse, New York, a city known for salt production in the 1800s. The town board formed in 1935, and a proclamation from Governor J. Bracken Lee made Syracuse a third-class city on September 13, 1950.

The growth since then is steep. Census counts show 4,658 residents in 1990, 9,398 in 2000, 24,331 in 2010 and 32,141 in 2020. The Census Bureau now estimates 39,909 for July 1, 2025. In 2020 the median age was 29.4 and 36.4% of residents were under 18, so the city is full of young families.

The road changed how people get around the west side of Davis County. It also changed interest in the land beside it. Syracuse is pursuing a 169-acre redevelopment area, the WDC Gateway Community Reinvestment Area, at Antelope Drive and 3000 West, for housing, retail and commercial use.

Syracuse has hot summers and a real winter. Summer highs often reach 95 degrees, the record high is 106 degrees on July 14, 2002, and the record low is minus 16 degrees on January 26, 1949.

The city averages about 24 inches of precipitation and about 39 inches of snow a year, and monsoon thunderstorms usually arrive from late July to mid-September. That mix means roofs, gutters and grading take a beating, and snow load and freeze-thaw cycles matter for older decks, driveways and sprinkler lines.

  • Check the roof and flashing after winter and after the monsoon season.
  • Look at grading near the foundation, since snowmelt and monsoon rain need somewhere to go.
  • Have the sprinkler lines blown out each fall before a hard freeze.

Syracuse is in the Davis School District, and the city also has the Syracuse Arts Academy charter campuses. Syracuse High School opened in 2007, Syracuse Junior High dates to 1960, and elementary schools include Cook (1979), Syracuse Elementary (1968), Bluff Ridge (1999) and Buffalo Point (2008).

School boundaries are usually one of the first questions a family asks, so look them up when you list or talk to a buyer. The Syracuse Arts Academy campuses are public charter schools with their own enrollment.

Because the city grew so quickly, houses built in the same stretch of years tend to need the same work around the same time, such as roofs and water heaters.

  • Minor home occupations are allowed in residential zones if they use no more than 300 square feet or 20% of the floor area.
  • Home occupation permits are not transferable and end when the applicant stops living at the address, so a buyer must apply again.
  • A business license is required unless the business is exempt under state law.

If you run a daycare, salon or similar home business out of the house, tell the buyer the permit does not carry over. For anything else, contact Syracuse City planning to confirm current rules.

Davis County property taxes follow the same Utah calendar as most counties: they are due November 30, and a late payment draws a 2.5% penalty or $10, whichever is greater, under Utah Code 59-2-1331. If November 30 falls on a weekend or holiday, the due date moves to the next business day.

The county mails a Notice of Assessors' Property Market Valuation at the end of July. The Davis County Commission acts as the Board of Equalization, and the county page gives September 15, 2026 as the late-appeal date, so file early.

  • You can appeal only the market value, not the tax rate.
  • Evidence can be closing documents, a certified appraisal, three or more comparable sales or proof of an error in the assessor's data.
  • Tax Administration is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101, Farmington, and can be reached at 801-451-3331.

Utah exempts 45% of a primary residence's value, up to one acre. Your title company prorates the current bill at closing.

Where is Roy, Utah, and what kind of city is it?

Roy is a residential city in Weber County, on the west side of Interstate 15, in the Ogden-Clearfield metro area. It is often described as a bedroom community, with a small number of local businesses and most residents commuting out to work.

The city sits at about 4,377 feet of elevation. Hooper lies to the west, West Haven to the north, Riverdale and Ogden to the east, and Clinton and Sunset in Davis County to the south. Roy has a mayor-council form of government.

For a seller, the layout matters because Roy is not one uniform market. Older homes on the eastern bench were built mostly in the 1950s and 1960s, while newer building moved west and south after about 2005, according to the city's history on Wikipedia. Two houses a mile apart can have very different ages, lot sizes and repair needs.

How did Roy grow, and why does that matter for an older house?

Roy grew mainly because of World War II and the military sites around it. The town was incorporated on March 10, 1937, and its population jumped from 868 in 1940 to 3,723 in 1950.

Roy housed workers from nearby installations, including Hill Air Force Base, the Navy Supply Depot (now the Freeport Center) and the Defense Supply Depot. Entry-level homes then filled much of the eastern bench through the 1950s and 1960s. Building continued at the western base of the hill from the 1980s.

That history explains what many Roy sellers are holding: mid-century starter homes that may still have original plumbing, older electrical panels, single-pane windows or an unfinished basement. Buyers financing with a loan often ask for repairs on those items. A cash buyer can take the house in its current condition instead.

Hill Air Force Base is the largest single influence on Roy's housing demand, and the base's north entrance is reached from I-15 exit 338, which puts Roy close to the gate.

Roy is served by I-15 at exit 338, which connects to Utah State Route 97 (5600 South), one of the city's main roads. The FrontRunner commuter rail has a Roy station that opened on April 26, 2008, along with the northern segment of the line.

Two sets of tracks cross the city at 2700 West, used by FrontRunner and the Union Pacific Railroad. Train noise is a real consideration for homes near that corridor, and a buyer or inspector may mention it.

Roy has cold winters and hot, dry summers, so roofs, furnaces and water lines take real wear. The mean daily high is 37 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 94 degrees in July, and the record low is minus 26 degrees.

Average annual precipitation is about 18.4 inches, with April or May usually the wettest month. Freeze and thaw cycles are the practical concern: they crack concrete, stress exposed pipes and shorten the life of asphalt shingles. A roof that is near the end of its life is one of the most common reasons a conventional buyer asks for a price cut.

Weber School District fully encompasses Roy. According to Wikipedia, the city has seven elementary schools, three junior highs and two high schools, and Roy High School competes in Region 5A.

The Roy City Recreation Complex on the high school campus has a pool, basketball courts, a weight room, racquetball courts and an indoor track. The Roy Aquatic Center is an outdoor complex. Roy Days, held in the first week of August around Roy West Park, includes a parade, a car show and fireworks.

Wikipedia notes that its school list is based on 2019 data and does not cover newer schools such as Haven Bay Elementary, Mountain View Junior High and West Field High, so confirm the current school for any specific address with the district.

Who owns and rents in Roy?

Roy is mostly owner-occupied. The 2020 census data summarized on Wikipedia counts 12,944 households, with 10,508 owner-occupied (81.2%) and 2,436 renter-occupied (18.8%), and 13,346 housing units at a 3.0% vacancy rate.

The median age is 31.8, and 41.5% of households have children under 18. The 2020 American Community Survey median household income listed there is $72,739.

Do you need a permit to fix up a Roy house before selling?

Yes, many repairs and additions in Roy need a permit, and the city requires that applications be filed online through its My City Inspector portal.

Roy's handout for one and two family dwellings lists what a plan set must include, such as a site plan, a footing and foundation plan, floor plans, elevations, insulation R-values and energy compliance documents. Initial plan review is meant to finish within 14 business days after plans are accepted, per state law. The handout does not list fees or which small projects are exempt, so call the Building Official before starting.

Unpermitted work is where many Roy sales stall. A buyer's lender or inspector may ask about a finished basement or a converted garage. Selling as-is to a cash buyer avoids the need to permit and finish work you no longer want to pay for.

Roy homes are taxed by Weber County, and the bill is due on November 30 each year, unless that date falls on a weekend or recognized holiday. Utah values property as of January 1 and exempts 45 percent of the market value of a primary residence, which covers the buildings and up to one acre of land.

Valuation notices are usually mailed around the end of July or the start of August. You have until September 15, or 45 days from the notice if that is later, to file an appeal. Weber County says late appeals are allowed only for severe circumstances such as a death in the family, a dire medical emergency or a factual error in the property description.

  • Taxes become delinquent on December 1.
  • Paid in full from December 1 through January 31, the penalty is the greater of $10 or 1 percent.
  • After that, the penalty is the greater of $10 or 2.5 percent, with interest running back to January 1.
  • Properties delinquent for five years are eligible for tax sale.

Ask the title company how the current year's tax will be split between you and the buyer at closing.

What does it cost to record a deed in Weber County?

The Weber County Recorder lists a first-page recording fee of $45.00 effective May 6, 2026, per HB 38, with no charge for additional standard pages. Pages larger than 8.5 by 14 inches carry a $2.00 surcharge, and each description over 10 adds $2.00.

What are your options for selling a house in Roy?

Roy sellers generally choose among a traditional listing, a sale by owner and a cash sale. Each has a different timeline and different out-of-pocket needs.

  • A listing can bring a wider pool of buyers, but it usually involves showings, repairs requested after inspection and the risk of a financing delay.
  • A sale by owner skips the agent but leaves marketing, contracts and disclosures to you.
  • A cash sale to a company like ours can close on a date you pick and the house is bought in its current condition, which suits inherited, tenant-occupied or neglected homes.

If your Roy house has deferred maintenance from decades of ownership, ask for a cash offer and compare it against what you would net after repairs, carrying costs and a longer wait. The decision is yours, and an offer carries no obligation.

September 15, or 45 days from the mailing of the valuation notice, whichever is later. File with the Weber County Board of Equalization. Late appeals are limited to severe circumstances.

No. A cash buyer can purchase a Roy house in its current condition. You may still want to tell the buyer about known problems such as roof leaks, an old furnace or unpermitted work.

Very close. The base's northern entrance is reached from I-15 exit 338, and Roy grew in the 1940s partly by housing workers from Hill AFB and nearby depots.

Yes, once you have the legal authority to sell, for example as the personal representative or as an owner on the title. Talk with a Utah attorney or title company about the paperwork, then ask for a cash offer if you want a quick closing.

The county's median household income was $77,057 in the source's figures, and 28.5% of residents 25 and older held a bachelor's degree. Provo and Orem together draw a commuting student population of more than 70,000 to BYU and UVU, which shapes traffic and rentals across the valley. Where is Washington, Utah, and how large is it?

Washington is a city in Washington County in the southwest corner of Utah, and it is part of the St. George metropolitan area. It sits at about 2,894 feet in elevation, a few miles east of St. George along Interstate 15.

The city is the second largest in the county. The 2020 census counted 27,993 people, up from 18,761 in 2010 and 8,186 in 2000. The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, shown at the top of this page, is 37,107.

Wikipedia lists the neighborhoods as old town Washington, Buena Vista, Green Springs and the Washington Fields area in the north. Older streets near the original townsite look quite different from the planned subdivisions that went up after 2000, so a seller on one side of town can face a very different buyer pool than a seller on the other.

What is the history of Washington City?

Washington was settled in 1857, when the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints sent 28 families to grow cotton in the desert. The mission was led by Robert Dockery Covington, a former Mississippi plantation owner, and a cotton mill operated in the town.

The name honors George Washington. The region picked up the nickname "Utah's Dixie" from the cotton-growing southeastern states, and the city has been using the shorter name "Washington City" in recent years. The old Washington School building now houses the city's historical museum.

For most of the twentieth century the town stayed small. Its population was 435 in 1950 and only 750 in 1970. Growth started in the 1980s and then sped up, which explains why so many houses in the city are less than twenty-five years old.

Water is the main long-term constraint in Washington County, and it shapes what a yard can look like. The Washington County Water Conservancy District reports that the county's population centers depend on the Virgin River basin and use more than 90% of the reliable annual supply.

In response, most cities in the county adopted rules that cap grass on new residential lots at 8% of the lot, with a separate cap for large lots. Grass is banned in park strips, in areas narrower than 8 feet and on slopes. Developers must use secondary or reuse water for irrigation where it is available, and potable water irrigation is banned from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. during summer months. The district also approved an excessive water use fee of $1.00 per 1,000 gallons for users above a set monthly volume.

The district's materials do not say how each rule applies in Washington City, so check the city's landscape and water conservation form before you change a yard. For a seller the practical point is simple: a large lawn on an older lot costs more to keep up, and buyers know it.

The same profile reports that the city added more than 3,300 homes between 2017 and 2021, including higher-density multifamily buildings near Exit 13. Any work you finish before listing should have a permit, and Washington City's Building Department issues them. The department handles single-family permits, additions, basement finishes, demolition, detached accessory buildings, garages and shops, sheds and patio covers, swimming pools and solar.

  • Construction hours are 6 a.m. to 10 p.m., and concrete may start at 3 a.m. from April through October.

  • The Building Department is at 111 North 100 East and can be reached at (435) 656-6326.

Unpermitted work, such as a finished basement, tends to surface when a buyer's inspector looks closely. Talk to the department before you list if you are unsure what was done to the house.

How do property tax and recording work when a Washington house sells?

Real property taxes in Washington County are due November 30 each year, and the lien follows the property, not the owner. The County Treasurer mails a notice to each owner, and title companies prorate the taxes at closing. Partial payments of $10 or more per parcel are accepted at any time, but the Treasurer's Office does not offer payment plans on delinquent taxes. Properties delinquent for at least five years can go to the county's tax sale held each May.

A primary residence in Utah is assessed on 55% of its market value because of a 45% residential exemption. A second home or an unoccupied house is taxed at the full value, which is worth checking if you own a house you no longer live in.

Deeds are recorded with the Washington County Recorder at 111 East Tabernacle Street in St. George. The posted fee is $45.00 per document plus $2.00 for each legal description over ten. The recorder does not accept recordings after 4:45 p.m. Mountain Time.

  • Competition from the large number of new houses built near Exit 13 and in the Washington Fields area.
  • Unfinished or unpermitted work discovered during a buyer's inspection.

Usually yes for additions, basement finishes, pools, solar and detached buildings. Washington City's Building Department issues permits through its City Inspect portal. Call (435) 656-6326 if you are not sure.

Where is Kearns, Utah?

Kearns is a city on the west side of the Salt Lake Valley, bordered by West Valley City to the north and west, Taylorsville to the east and West Jordan to the south. It covers 4.63 square miles, all land, at an elevation of about 4,530 feet.

Most of Kearns sits on the old bed of Lake Bonneville, the ancient lake that once filled the valley. A low rise called the Kearns-Benion hill climbs about 100 feet above the valley floor and runs northwest from the Jordan River toward the Oquirrh Mountains.

How did an Army base become Kearns?

Kearns began on May 1, 1942, as Kearns Army Air Base, a World War II training facility for the U.S. Army Air Forces named for Utah Senator Thomas Kearns. The land before then was dry farmland that had been set aside for universities and colleges.

The base was renamed Camp Kearns on January 1, 1944, and it was deactivated on August 15, 1946, when the Air Force transferred it to the State of Utah. Developers then built homes and businesses on the former base land, and Kearns grew into what Wikipedia calls the first suburb in Salt Lake County.

  • The base's streets and building foundations served as a template for the new neighborhoods.
  • A base chapel became part of Our Lady of Perpetual Help Catholic Church.
  • A base train station later served as a day-care center.
  • A base theater became part of Kearns Junior High School.

For sellers, the postwar origin matters. Kearns grew quickly in the mid to late 20th century, so a seller with a house from that era may be dealing with original roofs, wiring and plumbing. How did Kearns become a city?

Kearns became an incorporated city on May 1, 2024, under Utah House Bill 35, after years as an unincorporated community, a township and a metro township. Township status came on June 1, 2002, and voters approved a metro township in 2015, with that government taking effect January 1, 2017.

Residents resisted annexation by West Valley City and West Jordan during the 1990s, collecting enough signatures to keep the boundaries unchanged. Jesse Valdez is the first elected mayor of the City of Kearns. The mayor's office is at 4250 W 5415 S, by appointment, and the phone is 385-855-8375.

Day-to-day services still run through shared providers. Police and fire come through Unified Police and Unified Fire, and the Greater Salt Lake Municipal Services District handles building permits, business licensing, land use and zoning, code enforcement and stormwater. The district is at 860 W. Levoy Dr., Suite 300, Taylorsville, and its main number is 385-910-5600.

Coverage in the Taylorsville Journal said the city gained more tax options as a result, including a property tax and a telecommunications tax, and planned to create a redevelopment agency. Sellers who care about future taxes can watch the city's budget and agenda pages.

What is the Utah Olympic Oval, and why is it in Kearns?

The Utah Olympic Oval is a five-acre ice sports facility at 5662 South Cougar Lane in Kearns, built in 2001 for the 2002 Winter Olympics. It has Utah's only 400-meter speed skating oval, two international-size ice sheets and a four-lane, 442-meter running track.

It sits in Oquirrh Park, and the Oquirrh Recreation and Parks District runs the surrounding fitness center and programs, including public skating, Learn to Skate classes and curling. Kearns has also kept an annual parade each late July or early August, and a new Kearns Library opened in December 2020.

The Oval is a public venue as well as a former Olympic site, and the district lists skate rentals for people without their own skates.

Kearns is in the Granite School District, which also serves Holladay, West Valley City, Taylorsville and other Salt Lake County communities, and Kearns High School serves the city. Kearns Junior High School includes the former base theater.

South Valley Regional Airport, which began as Municipal Airport No. 2 near the base, was a small private-aviation field on the south border of the old base.

What does the Salt Lake Valley climate mean for a Kearns house?

Snow and long cold stretches put the roof and heating system to work each winter, and a seller who knows their ages is ready for the first question a buyer asks.

Earthquakes are the other concern. The Wasatch fault is Utah's most active, and the Utah Geological Survey says liquefaction is most likely in low-lying central parts of a valley, especially near lakes and stream corridors where groundwater is shallow. Susceptible soils are loose, young, sandy or silty deposits that are saturated within about 30 to 50 feet of the surface. Because Kearns lies on the Bonneville lake bed, a lot-specific check on the survey's maps makes sense.

  • Maps show general patterns only.

  • The last large quake on the Salt Lake City segment was about 1,400 years ago.

Where is Magna, Utah?

Magna is a city in Salt Lake County on the west side of the valley, just northeast of the Oquirrh Mountains and directly south of the Great Salt Lake. Its elevation is about 4,265 feet.

On the valley grid it sits between roughly 7200 and 9200 West and 2100 and 4100 South. Coon Creek drains from Coon Canyon and flows northwest through town toward the lake. SR-201 forms the northern edge as an expressway and meets I-80 to the west.

Magna's total area is listed as about 37 square miles, but most of that is water, with roughly 15 square miles of land.

How did a copper mill town become a city?

Magna began as a farming and ranching settlement and grew into a company town for copper processing. Pioneers started arriving in 1851, Abraham Coon ran a livestock ranch at the mouth of what is now Coon Canyon, and the community was first called Pleasant Green in 1868.

The turning point came in 1906, when D.C. Jackling's Utah Copper Company began construction of the Magna Mill. Jackling chose the name from the Latin word for great. The post office was renamed Magna in 1914, and the name was officially adopted on October 19, 1915.

  • 1924: the first building of Cyprus High School was completed.
  • 2001: Magna gained township status.
  • 2017: it became a metro township.
  • May 1, 2024: it became a city under Utah House Bill 35.

Older neighborhoods around Main Street carried names such as Greektown, Japantown, Snaketown and Little Italy. Newer single-family subdivisions went up south and east of the historic center during the 1970s.

Earlier census counts show how the town developed: 3,502 in 1950, 13,138 in 1980, 17,629 in 1990 and 22,770 in 2000. In 2020, about 56.2 percent of residents were non-Hispanic white and 34.4 percent were Hispanic or Latino of any race.

Subdivisions from the 1970s are now about fifty years old, so a seller of one of those homes may be weighing repairs to major systems before listing.

No deaths were reported and injuries were minor. Bricks fell from some buildings, about 145 historic structures were damaged, and Cyprus High School suffered some of the most significant damage.
